docs.text: Discord Check out our Discord server if you ever need help, want to meet new folks, or just want to talk anything radio. We also announce upcoming meetings and share information about upcoming deployments. MQTT Logging Channels MQTT messages are logged to Discord based on firmware and channel. If the sending node is linked to a Discord account, the message will show the owning user. Platform Channel Discord Channel Meshtastic MediumFast #logger Meshtastic All others #logger-other MeshCore Public #meshcore-logger MeshCore All others #meshcore-logger-other Discord Bot The NashMesh Discord bot lets you link your nodes, look up node info, manage flags, and share community resources. Slash Commands Slash commands are available from the bot and they allow for control of different features the bot offers. /linknode Link a Meshtastic or MeshCore node to your Discord account. If you don't provide a node ID, a modal will appear. With autocomplete enabled, you can also start typing a node name or hex ID. MH M3shHe4d Today at 2:30 PM /linknode Link Your Node Node ID * 8-char hex (Meshtastic) or 64-char key (Meshcore) Cancel Submit /unlinknode Remove the link between a node and your Discord account. Running the command with no node ID shows a dropdown of your linked nodes. Unlinking also clears any flags you've set for that node. Results are paginated if you have many nodes. Each node links to its page on Malla (Meshtastic) or the Analyzer (MeshCore). docs.text: What is MQTT? MQTT is a message-broker application that mesh nodes can connect to. By connecting to an MQTT server, all LoRa traffic your node sees is sent to our MQTT server where applications can pull and use it. MeshCore Meshtastic MeshCore MQTT Settings Key Value Host mqtt.nashme.sh Username meshdev Password large4cats MeshCore Analyzer Observer An Observer is a MeshCore node that reports packets it hears to the MeshCore Analyzer , helping map network coverage and reliability across the region. Observers can be repeaters, room servers, or companion devices, and can stop sharing data at any time. To set up your node as an observer, visit the Observer Onboarding page for step-by-step instructions. Use the following configuration to connect your observer to the NashMesh MQTT server: [general] iata = "BNA" [[broker]] name = "nashmesh" enabled = true server = "mqtt.nashme.sh" port = 1883 transport = "tcp" keepalive = 60 qos = 0 retain = true [broker.auth] method = "password" username = "meshdev" password = "large4cats" Experimental Observer Firmware Custom firmwares provided by Adam include observer functionality built directly into the firmware, no companion device or separate install needed. Both repeater and room server variants are available. Flash them from the web-based observer flasher, which stays up to date with the latest mainline and dev-branch builds automatically and lists all supported devices: Open the Observer Flasher For full documentation on all available settings and commands, see the MQTT Bridge Implementation docs . Radio Settings If this is a fresh flash or full erase, configure radio parameters for the NashMesh region: set radio 910.525,62.5,7,8 set tx 22 Device Identity Set your node's name and the Nashville IATA code: set name MyObserver set mqtt.iata BNA WiFi set wifi.ssid YourNetworkName set wifi.pwd YourPassword Add NashMesh and TennMesh Slot 1 is pre-configured for LetsMesh Analyzer. Replace slot 2 (LetsMesh EU) with TennMesh, and add NashMesh to slot 3: set mqtt2.preset tennmesh set mqtt3.preset nashmesh Reboot reboot After rebooting, verify your connections with: get mqtt.status If connected successfully, each configured preset will show ok . If you would like to still help with contributing your nodes data but do not want to connect to MQTT, please set OK to MQTT to true . This allows any MQTT gateway (a node connected to MQTT) to submit your data to our MQTT server. For more information on enabling OK to MQTT , check out Meshtastic's website . Meshtastic MQTT Settings Key Value Host mqtt.nashme.sh Username meshdev Password large4cats Topic msh/US/TN/Middle Primary Channel Uplink true Primary Channel Downlink false Ok to MQTT true Reminder It's preferred that MQTT is used only for collecting and displaying data from nodes. To keep the system running smoothly for everyone, we kindly ask that you leave MQTT downlink turned off on all public channels. This helps reduce unnecessary traffic on the server. Setup Images Provided are images showing each required change that is needed to setup MQTT. Mac OS X and iOS First navigate to the Settings tab. For iOS , this option is on the bottom of the screen. Then access the Channels option. Click on the Primary Channel to configure settings for it. Enable Uplink Enabled to allow MQTT to upload data the radio receives. Navigate to the Settings tab again. For iOS , this option is on the bottom of the screen. Click the MQTT module to configure settings for it. Set Enabled for MQTT and enable Encryption Enabled . If your radio depends on your phones cellular network for internet connectivity, enable MQTT Client Proxy . Set the Root Topic and MQTT server details. AI Assisted Page

Repeater (CLI) 1 Set all four radio params in one command, then reboot to apply. set radio 910.525,62.5,7,5 reboot get radio Frequency, bandwidth and spreading factor together define a LoRa channel . If even one differs from the rest of the mesh, your transmissions are unreadable: you'll hear nothing and no one hears you. MATCH → linked 910.525 910.525 62.5 · SF7 62.5 · SF7 MISMATCH → silence ✕ 910.525 915.0 62.5 · SF7 62.5 · SF7 Same frequency / bandwidth / spreading factor = a link. Any mismatch = mutual silence. Frequency NASHMESH 910.525 MHz BAND US 902–928 RULE must match exactly REBOOT to apply Frequency is the center of your radio channel: the precise point in the band where every transmission happens. Two radios on different frequencies are like two people on different stations: each is talking, neither hears the other. It's the first thing that has to match across the mesh. US ISM band · 902 – 928 MHz 902 928 910.525 the NashMesh channel, everyone tunes here 915? wrong freq = unheard Frequency is the exact point in the band where all transmissions happen. A node elsewhere is on a different station. Every node (companion or repeater) uses 910.525 MHz , inside the US 902–928 MHz ISM band that the USA/Canada preset selects. Load the preset first; it puts you in the right band, then confirm the exact frequency. Bandwidth NASHMESH 62.5 kHz A narrow bandwidth concentrates the signal's energy into less spectrum, so the receiver hears it more easily (more range and sensitivity), but the data rate drops and packets take longer. A wide bandwidth spreads energy out: faster data, but shorter reach and it scoops up more background noise. 62.5 kHz: narrow energy concentrated → sensitive · slower 500 kHz: wide energy spread → faster · shorter · noisier Narrow bandwidth packs the signal into less spectrum, easier to hear but slower. ★ NASHMESH 62.5 kHz · narrow reach longest speed slowest noise caught least Maximum sensitivity. Paired with fast SF7 for a reach/airtime balance. 125 / 250 kHz · mid reach medium speed faster noise caught more Common defaults on other meshes; quicker but less sensitive. 500 kHz · wide reach shortest speed fastest noise caught most High throughput, but pulls in more interference. Not used here. Spreading Factor NASHMESH SF7 RULE each +1 ≈ 2× airtime A higher SF stretches every symbol over more time, so a receiver can pull a weaker signal out of the noise; that's the extra range. The price: the packet occupies the air far longer ( every step up roughly doubles airtime ) and the data rate drops. Lower SF is the reverse: quick, light on the channel, shorter reach. SF7: short symbols fast · cheap airtime · shorter reach SF12: stretched symbols slow · heavy airtime · longest reach RANGE & AIRTIME → SF7 SF9 SF12 Each step up the dial roughly doubles time-on-air. NashMesh sits at the fast end: SF7. ★ NASHMESH SF7 fast end reach shorter airtime lowest speed fastest Brief packets, channel stays open. Repeater density supplies the distance. SF9 middle reach medium airtime ~4× SF7 speed medium A compromise some sparse rural meshes use. Heavier on the air. SF12 max range reach longest airtime ~30× SF7 speed slowest One slow packet can hog the channel. Wrong choice for a dense metro. ! SF is part of the channel, not a personal range boost It's tempting to read "higher SF = more range" and turn it up. But SF must match across the mesh; raise it alone and you simply vanish from the network. Distance is the repeaters' job; your job is short, cheap packets. Coding Rate DEFAULT CR5 (4/5) PER-PACKET · mixable LoRa adds redundant bits so a receiver can rebuild a packet that arrived partly garbled. Coding rate sets how much: CR5 (4/5) adds the least (one parity block per four data blocks), so packets are short and fast but tolerate the least corruption. CR8 (4/8) adds the most: tough against interference, but each packet takes far longer on the air. each packet = 4 data blocks + error-correction blocks CR5 (4/5) +1 · lightest, fastest CR6 (4/6) +2 CR7 (4/7) +3 CR8 (4/8) +4 · heaviest, toughest More parity = more interference survived, but every extra block is more time on the air. ★ DEFAULT CR5 4 / 5 overhead +25% airtime lowest resilience basic NashMesh default now that most links are reliable. CR6–7 4/6 – 4/7 overhead +50–75% airtime higher resilience more Middle ground for moderately noisy links. CR8 4 / 8 overhead +100% airtime highest resilience max For a marginal far node hardening its hop to the relay. ! Coding rate is per-packet: mixing is fine Unlike frequency, bandwidth and spreading factor, CR rides inside each packet's header. Any receiver reads it and adapts, so a CR8 node and a CR5 node hear each other perfectly. Default to CR5; leave a marginal far node on CR8 until its link firms up. Airtime TYPE shared resource RULE one TX at a time Every node on NashMesh shares one frequency, and radios can't talk over each other. So airtime (how long each packet occupies the channel) is a finite, shared budget. When too many packets compete for the same moment, they collide and are lost , and the whole mesh slows down. one channel · one transmitter at a time · time is the shared budget → packet long packet (high SF/CR) …full? overlap = COLLISION, both lost Every transmission claims a slice of the same timeline. Fill it up and packets collide. Spreading factor (biggest lever) each +1 ≈ 2× Narrow bandwidth halving BW ≈ 2× Heavier coding rate (CR8 vs CR5) ≈ 1.6× Bigger payload linear Re-flooding (every repeater repeats it) × nodes that hear it ! Airtime is the budget every other setting spends SF, bandwidth, coding rate, advert interval, hop count, loop detection: every one of them is ultimately a decision about how much of the shared timeline you consume. A flood mesh repeats each packet across many nodes, so the cost multiplies. Keep packets short and adverts sane, and the whole network stays fast for everyone. Duty Cycle FIRMWARE DEFAULT 50% RANGE 1–100% US no legal limit EU often 1–10% Duty cycle is the share of time a radio may spend transmitting. After each transmission the firmware holds the radio silent so its long-run on-air time stays under the cap. In the US 902–928 MHz band there's no fixed limit, so the firmware default of 50% is fine and we don't change it. Adverts & Routing Advert Intervals ZERO-HOP 60 min FLOOD 3h FLOOD range 3–168 h COST mesh-wide airtime A zero-hop advert reaches only nodes in direct range, a quiet local hello. A flood advert is rebroadcast by every repeater that hears it, propagating across the entire mesh so far-off nodes learn a route to you. ZERO-HOP: heard locally only YOU direct neighbours only · cheap FLOOD: repeated mesh-wide YOU every repeater rebroadcasts it · cost multiplies Zero-hop is a quiet local "I'm here." A flood advert propagates across the entire mesh, powerful and expensive. Zero-Hop set advert.interval 60 min Flood set flood.advert.interval 3h 3 hours is the firmware minimum, chosen while the mesh is still growing so new nodes discover routes fast. As density increases, raise the flood interval to reclaim airtime. set advert.interval 60 set flood.advert.interval 3 Discovery & Adverts ADVERT name · pos · key SIGNED anti-spoof CLIENTS on demand REPEATERS ~12 h flood A new MeshCore mesh feels dead by design. Nodes stay quiet; until two have each received the other's advert , they won't appear in each other's contacts, even on the same channel. An advert is a signed broadcast of your name, position, and public key : the handshake that makes private messaging possible. same channel, no advert → invisible YOU NODE ✕ not in each other's contacts after an advert → keys traded YOU NODE in contacts · DMs now possible On the same channel you can both use Public, but DMs need a traded advert first. Path Hash Mode RECOMMENDED 2-byte DEFAULT 0 (1-byte) NEEDS firmware 1.14+ PAIRS loop detection With a one-byte path ID there are only 256 possible values. On a mesh of hundreds of nodes, two repeaters inevitably share one, which muddies path diagnostics and triggers false loop-detection hits . Two-byte IDs (65,536) make collisions vanish. 1-byte path ID → only 256 possible slots. With hundreds of nodes, two land on the same one. A B A4 same hash ID → collision muddies path tracing · false loop-detection hits 2-byte = 65,536 slots → collisions effectively gone, routing stays clean. Two different repeaters sharing one 1-byte ID confuse routing and trip loop detection. Mode 0 1-byte unique IDs 256 max hops 64 collisions likely Legacy/universal. Fine for tiny meshes; collides on a big one. ★ RECOMMENDED Mode 1 2-byte unique IDs 65,536 max hops 32 collisions rare Clean routing & reliable loop detection. Needs firmware 1.14+. Mode 2 3-byte unique IDs 16.7 M max hops 21 collisions none Some run 3-byte; the 21-hop cap keeps floods more local. Companion: Gear → Experimental Settings → Default Path Hash Size → 2-Byte Repeater (CLI): set path.hash.mode 1 get path.hash.mode # 0=1B · 1=2B · 2=3B Loop Detection DEFAULT off PAIRS path hash mode NEEDS firmware 1.14+ Every repeater that hears a flood packet rebroadcasts it. If a faulty node keeps changing its path ID or a packet loops, the mesh can amplify it into a storm. Loop detection stops a healthy repeater from being an amplifier: it checks whether its own ID already appears in the path, and if so, drops the packet. Off default checking none Relies only on the dedup cache. Minimal very lax 1-byte 4+ hits 2-byte 2+ hits Rarely fires on a hop-limited mesh. Moderate balanced 1-byte 2+ hits 2-byte 1+ hit Catches real loops; false-positive risk stays low. Strict aggressive 1-byte 1+ hit 2-byte 1+ hit Risky on 1-byte paths; prefix collisions cause false drops. set loop.detect moderate get loop.detect # verify Multi-Acks NASHMESH 1 (on) DEFAULT 0 (off) HELPS remote admin When you send a command to a repeater remotely, the node acts on it and sends back an ACK. Over several hops, that single confirmation can die on the return path, leaving you unsure whether to resend. Multi-acks sends two confirmations instead of one , which dramatically increases the chance at least one arrives. set multi.acks 1 get multi.acks # 0 = off · 1 = on Timing & Signal Tuning RX Delay NASHMESH 3 DEFAULT 0 STATUS experimental EFFECT prefers clean paths In a flood, every repeater that hears a packet rebroadcasts it, including nodes that barely caught it. Those weak-signal repeats spend airtime and add congestion without improving delivery. RX delay adds a short processing delay scaled to signal quality: strong-signal copies are handled immediately; weak ones wait . By the time a weak copy would be processed, the packet has usually already propagated and it's dropped as a duplicate. set rxdelay 3 get rxdelay # experimental · range 0–20 TX Delay TUNED BY neighbor count DEFAULT 0.5 / 0.2 RANGE 0–2 SCOPE flood + direct When multiple repeaters hear the same flood packet and rebroadcast it at the same instant, their signals collide and the packet is lost . TX delay staggers when each repeater fires by adding a random wait window; the more neighbors competing, the wider the window needs to be. no spacing → fire together ✕ collision txdelay → random window ✓ clear Each repeater waits a random slice before repeating. More neighbors competing = wider window needed. Neighbors txdelay direct.txdelay 0 – 1 0.3 0.1 2 – 4 0.5 0.3 5 – 9 1 0.5 10 – 14 1.5 1 15 + 2 2 Check your count with the neighbors command, and revisit these as the node sees more over time. set txdelay 0.5 set direct.txdelay 0.3 AGC Reset Interval NASHMESH 4 sec DEFAULT 0 (off) STEP multiples of 4 FOR elevated nodes The SX1262 radio's automatic gain control can get stuck when hit by a strong out-of-band signal: a broadcast tower, a cell site, a nearby handheld. When it does, the noise floor pins at −120 dBm and the repeater goes deaf to weak signals until power-cycled. On an unattended hilltop node, that's a dead repeater nobody notices. Setting an interval makes the firmware reset the AGC on a timer so it recovers on its own, no reboot, no climb. set agc.reset.interval 4 get agc.reset.interval # seconds · 0 = off Reading Your Signal SOURCE stats-radio / app UNITS dBm · dB KEY METRIC SNR LoRa decodes below noise RSSI is how strong the incoming signal is. The noise floor is the ambient RF racket your receiver sits in. SNR is how far the signal stands above that noise (roughly RSSI minus the noise floor) and it's the single best gauge of link quality. Metric Good OK / edge Problem RSSI (dBm) ≳ −100 −100 to −118 ≲ −120 SNR (dB) ≥ 0 0 to −7 * < −7.5 * Noise floor (dBm) ≤ −120 −120 to −110 ≳ −105 * LoRa decodes below the noise floor; negative SNR still works. At NashMesh's SF7 the limit is about −7.5 dB. stats-radio # noise floor · last RSSI/SNR neighbors # who you hear, with SNR ! Watch SNR, not RSSI RSSI alone can fool you: a strong signal in a noisy spot still decodes badly. SNR already folds signal and noise together, so it's the truest read on link health. A negative SNR isn't automatically broken; LoRa can still pull signal out from under the noise, especially at higher spreading factors. Access & Messaging Access & Admin ADMIN full control GUEST read-only DEFAULT password = "password" REACH BLE / mesh Every repeater ships with the admin door unlocked: the default admin password is the literal word password , and it's publicly known. Until you change it, anyone can reconfigure your node. A separate guest password controls read-only access; leave it blank and anyone can read your node's info without logging in. The companion app's Remote Management reaches a node two ways: over Bluetooth when you're beside it, or across the mesh over LoRa when you're not, routed through your companion node with no internet involved. Owner Info COMMAND set owner.info FIRMWARE 1.12+ VISIBLE when guest blank TIP call sign + contact Your repeater is unattended and probably somewhere annoying to reach. When it misbehaves, other operators can see which node is the problem but have no way to reach you unless your contact is on the node itself. Owner info is that note, readable by anyone who can log in as a guest (which is everyone when the guest password is blank). Keep it brief: call sign or name, a contact method, and maybe a site name. The | character becomes a line break. set owner.info N0CALL | n0call@example.com | Site Name Direct Messages PRIVATE 1-to-1 END-TO-END encrypted REQUIRES traded advert A MeshCore DM is encrypted to one contact's public key : only they can read it. The first DM floods the mesh so it can reach the recipient regardless of where they are; once a route is established, subsequent messages follow that path. Two nodes can't DM each other until each has received the other's advert (the key exchange; see Discovery & Adverts). Channels TYPE group · shared key NASHMESH #tn-* · #bna-* PRIVATE own PSK A channel is a group room secured by one symmetric key (AES) that every member shares. Anyone with the key reads and sends; anyone without it just hears noise. Unlike a DM, a channel message is a flood: it spreads across every repeater with no delivery confirmation. Regional #tn-middle all of Middle Tennessee #tn-davidson your county (#tn-<county> for any nearby one) Topic #tenntalk statewide general chatter #ham amateur radio operators Bots & testing #bna-wx weather chatter + NashMesh wx bot #bna-bot · #bot automated traffic from bots #test human-to-human "can you hear me?" checks Regions See the current region layout across Tennessee on the live map. View Region Map ↗ Channels vs Regions CHANNELS 1-byte hash REGIONS 2-byte hash RULE access ≠ propagation It's easy to assume a channel name scopes where a message travels. It doesn't. MeshCore has two separate mechanisms, and mixing them up is the single biggest cause of flood traffic on a growing mesh. Channels "Who gets to read the message" Controls encryption & access group membership: Public vs #nashmesh . Changing the channel name isolates chat visibility, not radio propagation. Regions "Where the message gets forwarded" Controls repeater retransmission rules on the RF layer. Region names compile into a fixed 2-byte transport hash over the air. CHANNEL controls readership YOU B C ✓ reads ✕ static REGION controls distance YOU RPT EDGE ✕ forwards ✓ drops ✕ Channel decides who can actually decrypt a packet (B has the key, C doesn't). Region decides whether it's close enough on the RF layer to receive one at all. ! A channel does not limit RF propagation A message on a local channel still floods every distant repeater in range if its region isn't scoped. Long region names like us-tn-bna cost zero extra airtime bytes, so there's no tradeoff to scoping aggressively. Hierarchy & Propagation TOP-DOWN cascades to child-regions BOTTOM-UP blocked at parent-region Regions nest into a hierarchy, and traffic only cascades one direction. Top-down (allowed) Messages sent on a parent-region (e.g. us-tn ) automatically deliver down to child-region repeaters ( us-tn-middle , us-tn-bna ). Great for statewide alerts. Bottom-up (blocked) Local chatter sent on a child-region ( us-tn-bna ) is ignored by parent-region-only backbones ( us-southeast ). Protects wide-area airtime. top-down cascades ✓ bottom-up blocked ✕ us us-southeast us-tn us-tn-middle us-tn-bna nashmesh standalone Traffic cascades top-down through the hierarchy, but a parent-region-only backbone ignores traffic sent on a child-region. nashmesh sits outside the chain entirely. High-profile repeaters can carry multiple regions at once to bridge interstate corridors cleanly. Proposed Regions STATUS proposed FROM Aug 19, 2026 meetup Proposed region scope for repeaters serving Middle Tennessee, from top-down flood scope to local tactical use. SCOPE NARROWS → COST DROPS bna * — flood us — country us-southeast — region us-tn — state us-tn-middle — division us-tn-bna — metro nashmesh: standalone, local/tactical Each ring nests inside the next; pick the narrowest scope that still reaches everyone who needs to hear it. nashmesh is a separate standalone scope, not nested under any ring. Scope Region Channels Notes Flood * Any / default Unscoped flood across all repeaters unless denied Country us Public, #bot, #test Nationwide layer; wide-area & cross-country Country region us-southeast Public, #bot, #test Multi-state corridor: TN, GA, NC, AL, KY, VA State us-tn #tn, #tenntalk Statewide coordination across all Grand Divisions State division us-tn-middle #tn-middle Middle TN umbrella; flanked by us-tn-east & us-tn-west IATA metro us-tn-bna #bna-bot, #bna-wx, #bna-test, #wardriving Nashville metro, aligned with global MeshMapper Local / tactical nashmesh #nashmesh Dedicated local infrastructure or tactical ops Repeater Setup COMMAND region put SAVE region save Builds the top-down hierarchy of parent-regions and child-regions from the table above on a repeater, then saves it to flash. 1 If regions are already defined on your repeater , clear them first with region remove <name> for each one (child-regions before parent-regions), or use the Manage Region UI. See Editing Regions . 2 Build the hierarchy top-down: region put us region put us-southeast us region put us-tn us-southeast region put us-tn-middle us-tn region put us-tn-bna us-tn-middle 3 Add the standalone local/tactical scope and save to flash: region put nashmesh region save Editing Regions COMMAND region remove SAVE region save ! Removing a region with child-regions fails until the child-regions are gone A region can't be removed while another region still lists it as a parent-region. Remove the child-regions first (deepest first), then remove the region itself, then rebuild anything that pointed at it. Example: renaming us-tn-mid to us-tn-middle : region remove <name> — name is the exact region to delete. Fails if any other region still lists it as a parent-region. 1 Remove the child-region, then the parent-region being replaced: region remove us-tn-bna region remove us-tn-mid 2 Add the renamed parent-region and its child-region back: region put us-tn-middle us-tn region put us-tn-bna us-tn-middle 3 Save to flash and confirm the table: region save region list allowed Tips DISCOVER Tools → Discover Regions TAG Show Channel Message Region Scopes SCOPE Set Region Scope These live in the MeshCore app while connected to your Companion node — Repeaters are configured with the region CLI commands above, not through the app. Once repeaters in your area have Regions configured: Find nearby Regions: Tools → Discover Regions See Regions being advertised by repeaters in range and add them to your Companion. Show Region tags on messages: Settings → Message Settings → Show Channel Message Region Scopes This lets you see which Region each scoped message is using. Choose where your messages go: Channel Message Settings → Set Region Scope Select the Region you want that channel's messages to flood through from your Companion. ! Think of the Region Scope as choosing how far that channel's messages should travel through the mesh Bots Weather Bot HOME Nashville US wx WORLD gwx ON #bna-wx SCOPE us-tn-bna Message any of these on #bna-wx . wx uses NOAA (US only); gwx uses Open-Meteo (worldwide). Leave off a place and it defaults to Nashville. ! BNA-WX-BOT only replies on #bna-wx scoped to us-tn-bna Responses no longer flood out to other regions — if your repeater isn't in the us-tn-bna region, you won't see the bot's replies. Core checks test confirms bot got your message; reports direct/routed, SNR, path ping simplest liveness check → Pong! help lists all commands · help <cmd> for details Path & link diagnostics path decode and show the full routing path your message took tracer 01,7a,55 round-trip trace; bot hears the reply (use this one) trace 01,7a,55 one-direction trace; return may not be heard multitest listens 6 s and collects every unique path: how many routes are live Network utility prefix 1A look up repeaters by their 2-char prefix stats bot usage over the last 24 h channels list / inspect hashtag channels on the network Maintenance & Reference Flashing Over the Air (OTA) OTA flashing lets you update a repeater wirelessly without a USB cable. The device creates a temporary Wi-Fi access point and serves a browser-based update page. ! Supported node types OTA updates are only supported on Room Server/Repeater and Repeater nodes. Companion nodes must be flashed via USB. ! nRF52 devices: Bluetooth OTA only If your device uses an nRF52 chip, Wi-Fi OTA is not supported. Use nRF Device Firmware Update (iOS) or nRF Connect (Android) with the firmware .zip file instead of the .bin . ! Always use the un-merged .bin for OTA The un-merged .bin updates only the firmware and preserves your settings. The merged .bin fully erases the device; only use it for a clean start. 1 From the companion app, log into the node and run: start ota The device will create a Wi-Fi access point named MeshCore-OTA . 2 Connect your computer to the MeshCore-OTA network, then open a browser and navigate to: http://192.168.4.1/update Upload the un-merged .bin and wait for the upload to fully complete before navigating away. 3 Reconnect to the node in the companion app and confirm the firmware version: version Troubleshooting START radio match THEN discovery THEN signal LAST deafness Work down the list. Stop at the first thing that's wrong. 1 Same channel? freq · BW · SF · preset identical to the mesh 2 Traded adverts? you only see nodes you've swapped keys with; send a zero-hop advert 3 Signal above the floor? RSSI / SNR healthy; if weak: height, antenna, clear the path 4 Radio gone deaf? noise floor pinned at −120 dBm; AGC reset or reboot 5 One-way link? they hear you but you don't; check your RX: antenna, coax, local interference Symptom First move No one hears me confirm preset / radio params match exactly Contacts list is empty send an advert; the mesh is quiet by design Heard, but barely raise the antenna before anything else; height beats power Was fine, now deaf reboot or AGC reset; suspect a pinned noise floor They hear me, I don't the problem is on your receive side ! Re-send an advert after any move After changing location, antenna, or any radio setting, fire a zero-hop advert so neighbours re-learn your path. A stale route is one of the most common reasons a node is heard but messages don't get through. docs.text: TYPE shared resource RULE one TX at a time Every node on NashMesh shares one frequency, and radios can't talk over each other. So airtime (how long each packet occupies the channel) is a finite, shared budget. When too many packets compete for the same moment, they collide and are lost , and the whole mesh slows down. one channel · one transmitter at a time · time is the shared budget → packet long packet (high SF/CR) …full? overlap = COLLISION, both lost Every transmission claims a slice of the same timeline. Fill it up and packets collide. Spreading factor (biggest lever) each +1 ≈ 2× Narrow bandwidth halving BW ≈ 2× Heavier coding rate (CR8 vs CR5) ≈ 1.6× Bigger payload linear Re-flooding (every repeater repeats it) × nodes that hear it ! Airtime is the budget every other setting spends SF, bandwidth, coding rate, advert interval, hop count, loop detection: every one of them is ultimately a decision about how much of the shared timeline you consume. A flood mesh repeats each packet across many nodes, so the cost multiplies. Keep packets short and adverts sane, and the whole network stays fast for everyone.
docs.title: Airtime

docs.text: FIRMWARE DEFAULT 50% RANGE 1–100% US no legal limit EU often 1–10% Duty cycle is the share of time a radio may spend transmitting. After each transmission the firmware holds the radio silent so its long-run on-air time stays under the cap. In the US 902–928 MHz band there's no fixed limit, so the firmware default of 50% is fine and we don't change it.
docs.title: Duty Cycle

docs.text: ZERO-HOP 60 min FLOOD 3h FLOOD range 3–168 h COST mesh-wide airtime A zero-hop advert reaches only nodes in direct range, a quiet local hello. A flood advert is rebroadcast by every repeater that hears it, propagating across the entire mesh so far-off nodes learn a route to you. ZERO-HOP: heard locally only YOU direct neighbours only · cheap FLOOD: repeated mesh-wide YOU every repeater rebroadcasts it · cost multiplies Zero-hop is a quiet local "I'm here." A flood advert propagates across the entire mesh, powerful and expensive. Zero-Hop set advert.interval 60 min Flood set flood.advert.interval 3h 3 hours is the firmware minimum, chosen while the mesh is still growing so new nodes discover routes fast. As density increases, raise the flood interval to reclaim airtime. set advert.interval 60 set flood.advert.interval 3
docs.title: Advert Intervals

docs.text: ADVERT name · pos · key SIGNED anti-spoof CLIENTS on demand REPEATERS ~12 h flood A new MeshCore mesh feels dead by design. Nodes stay quiet; until two have each received the other's advert , they won't appear in each other's contacts, even on the same channel. An advert is a signed broadcast of your name, position, and public key : the handshake that makes private messaging possible. same channel, no advert → invisible YOU NODE ✕ not in each other's contacts after an advert → keys traded YOU NODE in contacts · DMs now possible On the same channel you can both use Public, but DMs need a traded advert first.
docs.title: Discovery & Adverts

docs.text: RECOMMENDED 2-byte DEFAULT 0 (1-byte) NEEDS firmware 1.14+ PAIRS loop detection With a one-byte path ID there are only 256 possible values. On a mesh of hundreds of nodes, two repeaters inevitably share one, which muddies path diagnostics and triggers false loop-detection hits . Two-byte IDs (65,536) make collisions vanish. 1-byte path ID → only 256 possible slots. With hundreds of nodes, two land on the same one. A B A4 same hash ID → collision muddies path tracing · false loop-detection hits 2-byte = 65,536 slots → collisions effectively gone, routing stays clean. Two different repeaters sharing one 1-byte ID confuse routing and trip loop detection. Mode 0 1-byte unique IDs 256 max hops 64 collisions likely Legacy/universal. Fine for tiny meshes; collides on a big one. ★ RECOMMENDED Mode 1 2-byte unique IDs 65,536 max hops 32 collisions rare Clean routing & reliable loop detection. Needs firmware 1.14+. Mode 2 3-byte unique IDs 16.7 M max hops 21 collisions none Some run 3-byte; the 21-hop cap keeps floods more local. Companion: Gear → Experimental Settings → Default Path Hash Size → 2-Byte Repeater (CLI): set path.hash.mode 1 get path.hash.mode # 0=1B · 1=2B · 2=3B
docs.title: Path Hash Mode

docs.text: DEFAULT off PAIRS path hash mode NEEDS firmware 1.14+ Every repeater that hears a flood packet rebroadcasts it. If a faulty node keeps changing its path ID or a packet loops, the mesh can amplify it into a storm. Loop detection stops a healthy repeater from being an amplifier: it checks whether its own ID already appears in the path, and if so, drops the packet. Off default checking none Relies only on the dedup cache. Minimal very lax 1-byte 4+ hits 2-byte 2+ hits Rarely fires on a hop-limited mesh. Moderate balanced 1-byte 2+ hits 2-byte 1+ hit Catches real loops; false-positive risk stays low. Strict aggressive 1-byte 1+ hit 2-byte 1+ hit Risky on 1-byte paths; prefix collisions cause false drops. set loop.detect moderate get loop.detect # verify
docs.title: Loop Detection

docs.text: NASHMESH 1 (on) DEFAULT 0 (off) HELPS remote admin When you send a command to a repeater remotely, the node acts on it and sends back an ACK. Over several hops, that single confirmation can die on the return path, leaving you unsure whether to resend. Multi-acks sends two confirmations instead of one , which dramatically increases the chance at least one arrives. set multi.acks 1 get multi.acks # 0 = off · 1 = on
docs.title: Multi-Acks

docs.text: NASHMESH 3 DEFAULT 0 STATUS experimental EFFECT prefers clean paths In a flood, every repeater that hears a packet rebroadcasts it, including nodes that barely caught it. Those weak-signal repeats spend airtime and add congestion without improving delivery. RX delay adds a short processing delay scaled to signal quality: strong-signal copies are handled immediately; weak ones wait . By the time a weak copy would be processed, the packet has usually already propagated and it's dropped as a duplicate. set rxdelay 3 get rxdelay # experimental · range 0–20
docs.title: RX Delay

docs.text: TUNED BY neighbor count DEFAULT 0.5 / 0.2 RANGE 0–2 SCOPE flood + direct When multiple repeaters hear the same flood packet and rebroadcast it at the same instant, their signals collide and the packet is lost . TX delay staggers when each repeater fires by adding a random wait window; the more neighbors competing, the wider the window needs to be. no spacing → fire together ✕ collision txdelay → random window ✓ clear Each repeater waits a random slice before repeating. More neighbors competing = wider window needed. Neighbors txdelay direct.txdelay 0 – 1 0.3 0.1 2 – 4 0.5 0.3 5 – 9 1 0.5 10 – 14 1.5 1 15 + 2 2 Check your count with the neighbors command, and revisit these as the node sees more over time. set txdelay 0.5 set direct.txdelay 0.3
docs.title: TX Delay

docs.text: NASHMESH 4 sec DEFAULT 0 (off) STEP multiples of 4 FOR elevated nodes The SX1262 radio's automatic gain control can get stuck when hit by a strong out-of-band signal: a broadcast tower, a cell site, a nearby handheld. When it does, the noise floor pins at −120 dBm and the repeater goes deaf to weak signals until power-cycled. On an unattended hilltop node, that's a dead repeater nobody notices. Setting an interval makes the firmware reset the AGC on a timer so it recovers on its own, no reboot, no climb. set agc.reset.interval 4 get agc.reset.interval # seconds · 0 = off
docs.title: AGC Reset Interval

docs.text: SOURCE stats-radio / app UNITS dBm · dB KEY METRIC SNR LoRa decodes below noise RSSI is how strong the incoming signal is. The noise floor is the ambient RF racket your receiver sits in. SNR is how far the signal stands above that noise (roughly RSSI minus the noise floor) and it's the single best gauge of link quality. Metric Good OK / edge Problem RSSI (dBm) ≳ −100 −100 to −118 ≲ −120 SNR (dB) ≥ 0 0 to −7 * < −7.5 * Noise floor (dBm) ≤ −120 −120 to −110 ≳ −105 * LoRa decodes below the noise floor; negative SNR still works. At NashMesh's SF7 the limit is about −7.5 dB. stats-radio # noise floor · last RSSI/SNR neighbors # who you hear, with SNR ! Watch SNR, not RSSI RSSI alone can fool you: a strong signal in a noisy spot still decodes badly. SNR already folds signal and noise together, so it's the truest read on link health. A negative SNR isn't automatically broken; LoRa can still pull signal out from under the noise, especially at higher spreading factors.
docs.title: Reading Your Signal

docs.text: ADMIN full control GUEST read-only DEFAULT password = "password" REACH BLE / mesh Every repeater ships with the admin door unlocked: the default admin password is the literal word password , and it's publicly known. Until you change it, anyone can reconfigure your node. A separate guest password controls read-only access; leave it blank and anyone can read your node's info without logging in. The companion app's Remote Management reaches a node two ways: over Bluetooth when you're beside it, or across the mesh over LoRa when you're not, routed through your companion node with no internet involved.
docs.title: Access & Admin

docs.text: COMMAND set owner.info FIRMWARE 1.12+ VISIBLE when guest blank TIP call sign + contact Your repeater is unattended and probably somewhere annoying to reach. When it misbehaves, other operators can see which node is the problem but have no way to reach you unless your contact is on the node itself. Owner info is that note, readable by anyone who can log in as a guest (which is everyone when the guest password is blank). Keep it brief: call sign or name, a contact method, and maybe a site name. The | character becomes a line break. set owner.info N0CALL | n0call@example.com | Site Name

docs.text: PRIVATE 1-to-1 END-TO-END encrypted REQUIRES traded advert A MeshCore DM is encrypted to one contact's public key : only they can read it. The first DM floods the mesh so it can reach the recipient regardless of where they are; once a route is established, subsequent messages follow that path. Two nodes can't DM each other until each has received the other's advert (the key exchange; see Discovery & Adverts).

docs.text: TYPE group · shared key NASHMESH #tn-* · #bna-* PRIVATE own PSK A channel is a group room secured by one symmetric key (AES) that every member shares. Anyone with the key reads and sends; anyone without it just hears noise. Unlike a DM, a channel message is a flood: it spreads across every repeater with no delivery confirmation. docs.text: COMMAND region remove SAVE region save ! Removing a region with child-regions fails until the child-regions are gone A region can't be removed while another region still lists it as a parent-region. Remove the child-regions first (deepest first), then remove the region itself, then rebuild anything that pointed at it. Example: renaming us-tn-mid to us-tn-middle : region remove <name> — name is the exact region to delete. Fails if any other region still lists it as a parent-region. 1 Remove the child-region, then the parent-region being replaced: region remove us-tn-bna region remove us-tn-mid 2 Add the renamed parent-region and its child-region back: region put us-tn-middle us-tn region put us-tn-bna us-tn-middle 3 Save to flash and confirm the table: region save region list allowed

docs.text: OTA flashing lets you update a repeater wirelessly without a USB cable. The device creates a temporary Wi-Fi access point and serves a browser-based update page. ! Supported node types OTA updates are only supported on Room Server/Repeater and Repeater nodes. Companion nodes must be flashed via USB. ! nRF52 devices: Bluetooth OTA only If your device uses an nRF52 chip, Wi-Fi OTA is not supported. Use nRF Device Firmware Update (iOS) or nRF Connect (Android) with the firmware .zip file instead of the .bin . ! Always use the un-merged .bin for OTA The un-merged .bin updates only the firmware and preserves your settings. The merged .bin fully erases the device; only use it for a clean start. 1 From the companion app, log into the node and run: start ota The device will create a Wi-Fi access point named MeshCore-OTA . 2 Connect your computer to the MeshCore-OTA network, then open a browser and navigate to: http://192.168.4.1/update Upload the un-merged .bin and wait for the upload to fully complete before navigating away. 3 Reconnect to the node in the companion app and confirm the firmware version: version
docs.title: Flashing Over the Air (OTA)

docs.text: START radio match THEN discovery THEN signal LAST deafness Work down the list. Stop at the first thing that's wrong. 1 Same channel? freq · BW · SF · preset identical to the mesh 2 Traded adverts? you only see nodes you've swapped keys with; send a zero-hop advert 3 Signal above the floor? RSSI / SNR healthy; if weak: height, antenna, clear the path 4 Radio gone deaf? noise floor pinned at −120 dBm; AGC reset or reboot 5 One-way link? they hear you but you don't; check your RX: antenna, coax, local interference Symptom First move No one hears me confirm preset / radio params match exactly Contacts list is empty send an advert; the mesh is quiet by design Heard, but barely raise the antenna before anything else; height beats power Was fine, now deaf reboot or AGC reset; suspect a pinned noise floor They hear me, I don't the problem is on your receive side ! Re-send an advert after any move After changing location, antenna, or any radio setting, fire a zero-hop advert so neighbours re-learn your path. A stale route is one of the most common reasons a node is heard but messages don't get through.

docs.text: Meshtastic We have some sane default settings that we strongly recommend you follow. If you are joining our network you may visit Discord and '/linknode !nodeid' in the logger channels. In the Middle TN Area, we have a few recommendations for configuration: (Make sure to read all the recommended settings) Flashing Your Device Make sure to keep your firmware up to date as you get started. The latest stable release, even if labeled Beta, is generally a very safe option. You can flash your device using the Meshtastic Web Flasher . LoRa Setting Value Region US Preset Medium Range Fast Max Hops (infrastructure nodes) 4 (up to 5) Max Hops (personal nodes) 6 (up to 7) Ignore MQTT (optional) Optional: Enable this to ignore traffic that may have been downlinked from MQTT (the internet) OK to MQTT (recommended) Recommended but optional: Enable this for your messages to be uploaded to MQTT (the internet). This is required for your messages to show up on the Discord logger, Malla, MeshInfo, or location on any maps. This helps us see where traffic flows, and troubleshoot issues. Channels Below are configuration settings for the 0 Primary Channel . Setting Value Name Left intentionally blank PSK AQ== Position Precision You may wish to turn off Positions & Location if you're not interested in broadcasting your location. If you wish to enable a precise location you can do so via any client other than iOS User Setting Value Long Name Something descriptive. Ex: Your name, Discord Handle, or Ham Callsign. You can even include an email or website (ProTip: put nashme.sh in your name so more people can find us) Short Name Max of 4 characters, something unique for you and that particular radio. This will be what's displayed in chat. You can even use emojis to spice things up. Is Licensed (not recommended) Not recommended. Do not enable unless you are a licensed Amateur Radio operators. (You will not be able to communicate with people on any of the default channels if you enable this) Device Roles Role Description CLIENT The safe, defacto role that is default. Perfect for your single primary node. It will relay messages it receives. CLIENT_MUTE Best for vehicles and any time you have more than 2 nodes in the same place. It will not relay messages. (It will still transmit its own packets) CLIENT_BASE Designed for stationary, high-elevation nodes (e.g., rooftops, attics) to act as a personal, privileged relay. It prioritizes rebroadcasting packets to/from specific "favorited" personal nodes, boosting signal reliability for weaker, indoor, or handheld devices while still acting as a regular client for general mesh traffic. Important note - You MUST favorite your personal indoor nodes to the Client Base node and vice-versa. ROUTER / REPEATER DO NOT use this role. There are a lot of considerations, and caveats, to using the official Router & Repeater roles. Remember: The Client or Client_Base role relays messages just fine. Module Configuration MQTT If you want to upload to the internet to help us with data logging, see MQTT - This can be on nodes with their own WiFi chips or on the go with MQTT client proxy from the phone app. Telemetry Setting Description Environment Telemetry Enabled Enables the environment telemetry sensors Device Metrics Update Interval How often to send Device Metrics over the mesh Environment Metrics Update Intervall How often to send Device Metrics over the mesh Tips Make sure to keep all automatic beacons like telemetry and position (if used on a stationary node) to 6 hours+ . If you want to send position while moving, use Smart Position , with minimum 10 minutes and distance trigger 100 to 130 . This helps keep the mesh network clean of background traffic that's of little use. Info Configuration guide was happily donated by bayme.sh .

docs.text: What is MeshCore? MeshCore is NashMesh's platform. It is a decentralized and encrypted mesh network using LoRa technology, built around two types of nodes: Companions and Repeaters. If you would like to see what nodes are in your area, check out our network map . Features Companion nodes transmit and receive user data and can optionally act as a repeater. Repeater nodes extend coverage by routing packets toward their destination. Unlike flood-based mesh networks, they do not retransmit every packet they receive. MeshCore uses AES encryption and supports up to a 64-hop limit for packets, making it well suited for communication that extends beyond a single region. Our current goal is to link up with the MeshCore network in East Tennessee and eventually across multiple states. Setup Our setup guide walks you through everything you need to configure your device and connect to the network. MeshCore Setup Guide → The Comms Channel has put together a great video going over MeshCore. Give it a watch to learn more!

docs.text: MeshCore Scaling Strategy: Region Scope & Channel Use for Middle TN Presented by jpryor223-kc8nno NashMesh Meetup, Wednesday, Aug 19, 2026 As our mesh grows, unscoped flood traffic and airtime saturation become real problems. This talk from our latest meetup covers how MeshCore's region system solves that, and proposes a region scope for Middle TN / NashMesh. Want the raw slide deck? Download the PDF . Let's coordinate on repeater region scope rollouts across Middle Tennessee and surrounding meshes — come chat in the NashMesh Discord .
